claim: Pitx2-Cre drives Cre expression in the left lateral plate mesoderm under the control of the Pitx2 asymmetric enhancer.
source: A transgenic mouse line that drives Cre expression in the left lateral plate mesoderm under the control of the Pitx2 asymmetric enhancer (Shiratori et al., 2006) was combined with an R26LSL-DTR strain that expresses diphtheria toxin receptor (DTR) following Cre-induced recombination (Buch et al., 2005) (Pit::DTR mice).
evidence: The statement cites published work (Shiratori et al., 2006) describing the Pitx2-Cre transgenic line.

claim: Pit::DTR mice expressed DTR primarily in the left but not right limb mesenchyme, excluding muscles and blood vessels.
source: As expected, Pit::DTR mice expressed DTR primarily in the left but not right limb mesenchyme, excluding muscles and blood vessels (Figure 1A'; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemical data shown in Figure 1A' and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: A single systemic injection of DT at P1 resulted in cell death in the left hindlimb mesenchyme between 1 and 3 days post-injection.
source: To model an acute injury at birth, a single systemic injection of DT was administered at postnatal day (P) 1 (P1-Pit::DTR model), resulting in cell death in the left hindlimb mesenchyme between 1 and 3 days post-injection (dpi), with little in the right limb (Figure 1B and not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Cell death was not detected in the left GPs of the tibia and femur of P1-Pit::DTR mice.
source: Unexpectedly, however, cell death was not detected in the left GPs of the tibia and femur of P1-Pit::DTR mice, and the front of apoptotic cells only reached the outermost layers of the prospective articular cartilage and perichondrium from P2 to P5 (Figure 1B–B''; the proportion of cells undergoing cell death in the perichondrial groove of Ranvier was 18 ± 7% at P2, n = 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 1B–B'' and quantification of cell death.

claim: DT cannot diffuse efficiently into the postnatal GP, which is avascular and a very effective barrier to the diffusion of molecules larger than 10 kDa.
source: It is likely that DT (a ~60 kDa molecule) cannot diffuse efficiently into the postnatal GP, which is avascular (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) and a very effective barrier to the diffusion of molecules larger than 10 kDa (Williams et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to published work (Williams et al., 2007) and data showing the GP is avascular (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).

claim: At the highest concentration of DT (500 ng/ml), cell death was triggered in some cells in the core of the GP in cultured tibiae.
source: We found that at the highest concentration of DT, cell death was triggered in some cells in the core of the GP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), confirming that postnatal chondrocytes can respond to DT.
evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL staining data from cultured tibiae shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Cell death in the surrounding tissues resulted in ~5% (0.3mm) length difference between the left and right femora and tibiae at three dpi.
source: Interestingly, despite sparing of the GP in the P1-Pit::DTR model, cell death in the surrounding tissues resulted in ~5% (0.3mm) length difference between the left and right femora and tibiae at three dpi that was not observed in control animals (either DT-injected Pitx2-Cre; R26+/+ or PBS-injected Pit::DTR mice), and that plateaued at ~11% (~2 mm) after 9 weeks (Figure 1C, n = 4 control and 9 experimental mice at 3dpi, n = 16 and 7 respectively at 63-69dpi).
evidence: The claim is supported by bone length measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The left specific reduction in bone growth plateaued at ~11% (~2 mm) after 9 weeks.
source: Interestingly, despite sparing of the GP in the P1-Pit::DTR model, cell death in the surrounding tissues resulted in ~5% (0.3mm) length difference between the left and right femora and tibiae at three dpi that was not observed in control animals (either DT-injected Pitx2-Cre; R26+/+ or PBS-injected Pit::DTR mice), and that plateaued at ~11% (~2 mm) after 9 weeks (Figure 1C, n = 4 control and 9 experimental mice at 3dpi, n = 16 and 7 respectively at 63-69dpi).
evidence: The claim is supported by bone length measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The forelimbs were not affected by DT injection in P1-Pit::DTR mice, as they express little DTR.
source: The forelimbs were not affected, as they express little DTR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by DTR immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: P1-Pit::DTR animals showed a transient systemic growth reduction with respect to control littermates, both in body weight and length of the right long bones.
source: The left specific reduction in bone growth took place on top of a transient systemic growth reduction with respect to control littermates, both in body weight and length of the right long bones (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by body weight and bone length measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: The systemic growth reduction was likely caused by cell death in a region of the heart where Pitx2-Cre drives DTR expression.
source: The systemic growth reduction was likely caused by cell death in a region of the heart where Pitx2-Cre drives DTR expression (Shiratori et al., 2006) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–C'), as we observed that P1-Pit::DTR animals were lethargic for ~4 days after DT injection, including severe (sometimes lethal) hypophagia.
evidence: The claim is supported by DTR expression and TUNEL staining data in the heart shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–C', and by citation to Shiratori et al., 2006.

claim: The GPs of P1-Pit::DTR mice at P5 were smaller than in control animals.
source: As a consequence, the GPs of P1-Pit::DTR mice at P5 were smaller than in control animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–E').
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–E'.

claim: Agcn1 and Col2a1 expression was downregulated in both the left and right GPs of P1-Pit::DTR mice at P5 compared to controls.
source: At the molecular level, one difference found between control and P1-Pit::DTR mice at P5 was a decrease in the synthesis of ECM in both the left and right GPs of P1-Pit::DTR mice, as Agcn1 and Col2a1 expression was downregulated compared to controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: By the end of the longitudinal growth period, the lengths of the right but not the left long bones had normalized in P1-Pit::DTR mice.
source: Importantly, by the end of the longitudinal growth period, the lengths of the right but not the left long bones had normalized in P1-Pit::DTR mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), demonstrating the left-specific growth reduction is independent of the transient systemic effect.
evidence: The claim is supported by bone length measurements shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The left/right ratio of EdU incorporation in the proliferative zone of the proximal tibial GPs was reduced in the P1-Pit::DTR model compared to control animals at P3.
source: Indeed, the left/right ratio of EdU incorporation in the proliferative zone (PZ) of the proximal tibial GPs was reduced in the P1-Pit::DTR model compared to control animals at P3 (Figure 2A, n = 4 control and 7 experimental animals).
evidence: The claim is supported by EdU incorporation data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: At P4-P5, there was an obvious decrease in the height of the HZ but not the PZ in P1-Pit::DTR mice.
source: Moreover, at P4-P5 we observed an obvious decrease in the height of the HZ but not the PZ (Figure 2B), as further revealed by in situ hybridization for the chondrocyte maturation marker Col10a1 (Figure 2C, n = 3) and hematoxylin and eosin staining (Figure 2D, n = 4 control, 4 experimental).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological measurements and in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2B, 2C, and 2D.

claim: The formation and expansion of the secondary ossification centers in the left bones of P1-Pit::DTR mice at P4-5 was slightly delayed and progressed more slowly as compared to the right bones.
source: In addition, the formation and expansion of the secondary ossification centers in the left bones of P1-Pit::DTR mice at P4-5 was slightly delayed and progressed more slowly as compared to the right bones (Figure 2E–F, n = 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by skeletal staining and quantification data shown in Figure 2E–F.

claim: HTCs did not display increased EGFR signaling in P1-Pit::DTR mice.
source: Importantly, HTCs did not display increased EGFR signaling (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), which can be activated by DTR shedding (Xu et al., 2004) and impairs terminal chondrocyte differentiation and cartilage remodeling (Zhang et al., 2011; Hall et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and citations to Xu et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2011; Hall et al., 2013.

claim: Most osteoprogenitors in the perichondrium of P1-Pit::DTR animals were not TUNEL+.
source: In addition, the potential ablation of osteoprogenitors in the perichondrium of P1-Pit::DTR animals was an unlikely cause of the reduced bone growth, as most of these cells were not TUNEL+ in our model (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–C').
evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–C'.

claim: Near-complete ablation of osteoprogenitors using an Sp7 (Osx)-driven Cre (Osx::DTR model) failed to impair longitudinal bone growth, although it did reduce cortical thickness.
source: Moreover, a near-complete ablation of osteoprogenitors using an Sp7 (Osx)-driven Cre (Osx::DTR model) failed to impair longitudinal bone growth, although it did reduce cortical thickness (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by bone length and cortical thickness measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F.

claim: Increased cell death was not detected in the osteochondral junction of P1-Pit::DTR mice.
source: Finally, we did not detect increased cell death in the osteochondral junction that could explain the observed HZ shortening (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Ihh expression was reduced in the left compared to right GPs at P3 in P1-Pit::DTR mice.
source: Significantly, we found that Ihh expression was reduced in the left compared to right GPs at P3, as was the expression of the HH target gene Gli1 (Figure 3A–A', n = 14/16 and 8/10, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A–A'.

claim: Gli1 expression was reduced in the left compared to right GPs at P3 in P1-Pit::DTR mice.
source: Significantly, we found that Ihh expression was reduced in the left compared to right GPs at P3, as was the expression of the HH target gene Gli1 (Figure 3A–A', n = 14/16 and 8/10, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3A–A'.

claim: Pthlh expression was not changed in P1-Pit::DTR mice.
source: We did not, however, observe a change in expression of the IHH target Pthlh (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by X-gal staining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Treatment with an SHP2 inhibitor rescued Ihh expression but did not rescue bone growth in P1-Pit::DTR mice.
source: Given that the phosphatase SHP2 negatively modulates Ihh levels in cultured chondrocytes (Guan et al., 2014), we treated P1-Pit::DTR pups with an SHP2 inhibitor from P1 to P3. While the treatment rescued Ihh expression, it did not rescue bone growth (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–C'), suggesting that other parallel signaling pathways were disturbed.
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization and bone length measurement data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–C', and citation to Guan et al., 2014.

claim: p-S6 levels were reduced in the left PZ and pre-HZ from P3 until at least P5 in P1-Pit::DTR mice.
source: Since mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) is implicated in chondrocyte maturation and hypertrophy (Lai et al., 2013; Phornphutkul et al., 2008; Srinivas et al., 2009), we next performed immunohistochemical detection of p-S6, a readout of mTORC1 activity, and found that indeed p-S6 levels were reduced in the left PZ and pre-HZ from P3 until at least P5 (Figures 3B and 4, n = 19/23, 7/8 and 3/3 at P3, P4 and P5, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figures 3B and 4, and citations to Lai et al., 2013; Phornphutkul et al., 2008; Srinivas et al., 2009.

claim: Treatment with the mTORC1 inhibitor rapamycin mimicked the downregulation of p-S6 in the right GP of P1-Pit::DTR mice and also in both hindlimbs of WT pups.
source: We further found that this downregulation could be mimicked in the right GP of P1-Pit::DTR mice and also in both hindlimbs of WT pups by treatment with the mTORC1 inhibitor rapamycin, which also stunts overall growth (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and bone length measurement data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–E.

claim: FGF signaling was not increased in any region of the left GP of P1-Pit::DTR mice at P3.
source: Since FGFs secreted by the perichondrium negatively regulate chondrocyte proliferation and early hypertrophy (Liu et al., 2002; Karuppaiah et al., 2016), we tested whether FGF signaling was altered, but did not detect an increase in FGF signaling in any region of the left GP of P1-Pit::DTR mice at P3 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–B').
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–B', and citations to Liu et al., 2002; Karuppaiah et al., 2016.

claim: Fgfr3 expression was downregulated in the region of the left GP where the secondary ossification center forms in P1-Pit::DTR mice.
source: On the contrary, Fgfr3 expression was downregulated in the region of the left GP where the secondary ossification center forms, suggesting Fgfr3 could be involved in the observed delayed formation and expansion of this structure.
evidence: The claim is based on in situ hybridization data (referenced in the context of Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–B').

claim: MCP5 mRNA or protein was not detected in P1-Pit::DTR mice at P3.
source: Moreover, decreased TGFβR2 signaling in the joint region has been shown to impair chondrocyte hypertrophy at embryonic stages via increased expression of the cytokine MCP5 (Longobardi et al., 2012), but we were not able to detect MCP5 mRNA or protein in our model at P3.
evidence: The claim is based on the absence of detection of MCP5 in the experimental model, and cites Longobardi et al., 2012.

claim: RNA and protein levels of the WNT target Lef1 were upregulated in the RZ of the left P1-Pit::DTR GP compared to right.
source: On the other hand, RNA and protein levels of the WNT target Lef1 were upregulated in the RZ of the left P1-Pit::DTR GP compared to right (Figure 3C; see also Figure 4—figure supplement 2, n = 5 at P3, 4 at P4, 3 at P5), which might impair PTHLH signaling and chondrocyte differentiation, as described (Ray et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2, and citations to Ray et al., 2015; Guo et al., 2009.

claim: Igf1 was highly expressed in the right infrapatellar fat pad (IPFP) but was extremely and specifically downregulated in the left IPFP of P1-Pit::DTR mice at 2-3dpi.
source: Interestingly, we found that while Igf1 was highly expressed in the right infrapatellar fat pad (IPFP), an extra-synovial adipose tissue located between the femur and the tibia, it was extremely and specifically downregulated in the left IPFP of P1-Pit::DTR mice at 2-3dpi (Figure 4A, n = 10/12), and recovered by 4dpi (Figure 4A', n = 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4A and 4A'.

claim: Igf1 expression recovered in the left IPFP of P1-Pit::DTR mice by 4dpi.
source: Interestingly, we found that while Igf1 was highly expressed in the right infrapatellar fat pad (IPFP), an extra-synovial adipose tissue located between the femur and the tibia, it was extremely and specifically downregulated in the left IPFP of P1-Pit::DTR mice at 2-3dpi (Figure 4A, n = 10/12), and recovered by 4dpi (Figure 4A', n = 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4A'.

claim: Igf1 expression was not consistently altered in other tissues, such as the perichondrium, the muscle bundles or cells in the metaphyseal region.
source: Furthermore, Igf1 expression was not consistently altered in other tissues, such as the perichondrium, the muscle bundles or cells in the metaphyseal (shaft) region (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Only minor to no changes were detected in the expression of Igf2 or the main IGF receptor gene Igf1r in the GP or surrounding tissues.
source: Similarly, we only detected minor to no changes in the expression of Igf2 or the main IGF receptor gene Igf1r in the GP or surrounding tissues (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C), indicating that the IPFP was specifically affected by the insult.
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: Differential expression of SOCS3 between the left and right GPs was not detected at P2 or P3 in P1-Pit::DTR mice.
source: In particular, since injury-induced inflammation (see below) could conceivably increase expression of suppressor of cytokine signaling 3 (SOCS3), which is known to exert a negative influence on IGF signaling (Ahmed and Farquharson, 2010), we performed SOCS3 immunohistochemistry on P1-Pit::DTR knee sections. However, we could not detect differential expression between the left and right GPs at P2 or P3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that it is the reduced availability of IGF1 from the IPFP that causes some of the signaling changes observed in the left GP.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, and citation to Ahmed and Farquharson, 2010.

claim: Exogenous IGF1 provided by intraarticular injections in P1-Pit::DTR pups (P1-P3) consistently rescued mTORC1 signaling in the PZ and pre-HZ of the GPs.
source: To test this possibility, we provided exogenous IGF1 to the left knee region by intraarticular injections in P1-Pit::DTR pups (P1-P3), and found that indeed mTORC1 signaling was consistently rescued in the PZ and pre-HZ of the GPs (Figure 4B' top, n = 5 P3-P5 pups).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4B'.

claim: Ihh and Fgfr3 expression were rescued in IGF1-injected P1-Pit::DTR animals.
source: Curiously, Ihh and Fgfr3 expression were also rescued in these animals (Figure 4B' bottom, n = 3 at P3, and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), suggesting that both genes are downstream of IGF signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4B' and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Left-specific neutrophil recruitment was observed in the IPFP at P2-P4 in P1-Pit::DTR mice and had mostly receded by P5.
source: We observed left-specific neutrophil recruitment at P2-P4 that had mostly receded by P5, thus precisely correlating with transient Igf1 downregulation (Figure 4C–C' n = 5, 5, 4, 5 at P2, P3, P4, P5).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4C–C'.

claim: Macrophages were additionally recruited to the left IPFP in P1-Pit::DTR mice.
source: Moreover, macrophages, already very abundant in the IPFP in resting conditions, were additionally recruited to the left IPFP (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–A').
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–A'.

claim: Neutrophil blockade with the NIMP-R14 neutralizing antibody significantly correlated with partial recovery of Igf1 expression in the IPFP.
source: As neutrophils are an important feature of joint inflammatory diseases (Wright et al., 2010; Wipke and Allen, 2001), we tested whether neutrophils were responsible for Igf1 downregulation by blocking their recruitment with the NIMP-R14 neutralizing antibody (Lopez et al., 1984) during P1-P3 in P1-Pit::DTR mice. Neutrophil blockade was effective for at least 14 hr (Figure 4D, n = 3), and significantly correlated with partial recovery of Igf1 expression in the IPFP (Figure 4D', n = 4), without inhibiting cell death in this region (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4D', and citations to Wright et al., 2010; Wipke and Allen, 2001; Lopez et al., 1984.

claim: The recovery of Igf1 expression after neutrophil blockade correlated with increased levels of p-S6 and Ihh in the pre-HZ.
source: Importantly, the recovery of Igf1 expression correlated with increased levels of p-S6 and Ihh in the pre-HZ (Figure 4D'', n = 3, and not shown), demonstrating that proper signaling in the pre-HZ requires IGF1 production from the IPFP.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4D''.

claim: LPS injection into the joint of WT animals caused a strong local recruitment of neutrophils to the IPFP and led to downregulation of Igf1 in the areas with highest accumulation of neutrophils.
source: To further probe the role of immune-cell recruitment in Igf1 downregulation, we injected lipopolysaccharide (LPS) into the joint of WT animals, which caused a strong (but patchy) local recruitment of neutrophils to the IPFP. Of significance, this recruitment led to the predicted downregulation of Igf1 in the areas with highest accumulation of neutrophils (Figure 4—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3C.

claim: LPS-induced neutrophil recruitment led to Igf1 downregulation in the absence of cell death.
source: This effect took place in the absence of cell death (Figure 4—figure supplement 3D), suggesting that immune cells (probably neutrophils) secrete factors that reduce Igf1 expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3D.

claim: TNFα-expressing cells (some of them neutrophils) were present in the left and not the right IPFP in P1-Pit::DTR mice at P2.
source: Notably, we found that TNFα-expressing cells (some of them neutrophils) were present in the left and not the right IPFP in P1-Pit::DTR mice at P2, and that neutrophils accumulated TNFα in what seemed to be the Golgi apparatus (Figure 4C''').
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4C'''.

claim: TNFα has been shown to reduce Igf1 expression in vascular smooth muscle.
source: TNFα has been shown to reduce Igf1 expression in vascular smooth muscle (Anwar et al., 2002), raising the possibility that this cytokine is in part responsible for the observed Igf1 downregulation in the left IPFP of P1-Pit::DTR mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Anwar et al., 2002.

claim: Partial restoration of Igf1 expression by neutrophil blockade did not rescue Fgfr3 expression.
source: Interestingly, partial restoration of Igf1 expression by neutrophil blockade did not rescue Fgfr3 expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that full restoration of Igf1 is necessary for normal Fgfr3 expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Neither IGF1 injection nor neutrophil blockade were sufficient to rescue the decreased left bone growth at P4.
source: Despite IGF1 supplementation rescuing several critical pathways, neither IGF1 injection nor neutrophil blockade were sufficient to rescue the decreased left bone growth at P4 (Figure 4E–F, n = 5 experimental and 5 control animals for each treatment), indicating that an IGF1-independent pathway also contributes to the growth defect.
evidence: The claim is supported by bone length measurement data shown in Figure 4E–F.

claim: Expression of Lef1 in the left GP remained upregulated after IGF1 injection or neutrophil blockade.
source: Indeed, expression of Lef1 in the left GP remained upregulated after IGF1 injection or neutrophil blockade (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–B), raising the possibility that increased LEF1 activity contributes to the growth defect.
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: Expression of Early growth response gene 1 (Egr1) was increased in the left IPFP and pAC of P1-Pit::DTR mice at P2 (1dpi).
source: Given the importance of the immediate-early damage response upon injury, we tested its activation and indeed detected it in the left joint region of P1-Pit::DTR mice, not only in the IPFP but also in the prospective articular cartilage (pAC). Specifically, we observed that expression of Early growth response gene 1 (Egr1) was increased in the left IPFP and pAC of P1-Pit::DTR mice at P2 (1dpi) (Figure 5A, n = 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Egr1 expression in the left IPFP receded by P3, but remained highly upregulated in the left pAC through P4, receding by P5.
source: Egr1 expression in the left IPFP receded by P3, but remained highly upregulated in the left pAC through P4, receding by P5 (Figure 5B–C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B, n = 3, 2, 2, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5B–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: p-S6 expression was upregulated in the left pAC at P3 and P4 and receded by P5.
source: Interestingly, p-S6 expression, while downregulated in the pre-HZ (Figures 3 and 4), was upregulated in the left pAC at P3 and P4 and receded by P5 (Figure 5B–C, n = 33, 14 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B', n = 2), suggesting transiently increased mTORC1 signaling in this region, as observed in osteoarthritis (Pal et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5B–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B', and citation to Pal et al., 2015.

claim: Ectopic expression of Hif2a was detected in the left pAC of P1-Pit::DTR mice.
source: For example, we detected ectopic expression of Hif2a (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), which has a prominent role in cartilage destruction during osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis (Ryu et al., 2014; Husa et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, and citations to Ryu et al., 2014; Husa et al., 2010.

claim: Il6 was upregulated in the left pAC of P1-Pit::DTR mice.
source: In addition, Il6, one of the main mediators of Hif2a-dependent cartilage destruction (Ryu et al., 2014), was upregulated in the left pAC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), and was the likely cause of the ectopic JAK1/2-dependent expression of p-STAT3 we detected in the pAC at P3 and P4 (Figure 5B–C, n = 13 and 3; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and that receded by P5 (not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, and citation to Ryu et al., 2014.

claim: Ectopic JAK1/2-dependent expression of p-STAT3 was detected in the pAC at P3 and P4 in P1-Pit::DTR mice and receded by P5.
source: In addition, Il6, one of the main mediators of Hif2a-dependent cartilage destruction (Ryu et al., 2014), was upregulated in the left pAC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), and was the likely cause of the ectopic JAK1/2-dependent expression of p-STAT3 we detected in the pAC at P3 and P4 (Figure 5B–C, n = 13 and 3; Figure 5—figure supplement 1C), and that receded by P5 (not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5B–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Expression of Egr1, p-S6 and p-STAT3 in the pAC was not due to inflammation in the IPFP, as neutrophil blockade or injection of IGF1 did not preclude activation of the injury response in the pAC of P1-Pit::DTR mice.
source: Importantly, expression of Egr1, p-S6 and p-STAT3 was not due to inflammation in the IPFP, as neutrophil blockade or injection of IGF1 did not preclude activation of the injury response in the pAC of P1-Pit::DTR mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Histological analysis revealed extensive and persistent cell loss in the pAC/AC from P4 to at least P27.
source: Associated with the injury response, histological analysis revealed extensive and persistent cell loss in the pAC/AC from P4 to at least P27 (Figure 5D–E, n = 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 5D–E.

claim: Most signaling changes in the pAC extended beyond the area of cell death, almost reaching into the RZ of the GP.
source: Of note, most signaling changes extended beyond the area of cell death (i.e. the pAC), almost reaching into the RZ of the GP (compare TUNEL and p-STAT3 in Figure 5B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of TUNEL and p-STAT3 staining in Figure 5B–C.

claim: Cells in the pAC/AC do not normally give rise to GP chondrocytes.
source: Since cells in the pAC/AC do not normally give rise to GP chondrocytes (Kozhemyakina et al., 2015), this set of results raised the possibility that the injury response in the pAC triggers a paracrine-signaling cascade that contributes to the signaling defects observed in the RZ.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Kozhemyakina et al., 2015.

claim: In vivo treatment with the JAK1/2 inhibitor ruxolitinib precluded p-STAT3 and LEF1 upregulation in the articular region of P1-Pit::DTR mice.
source: Significantly, in vivo treatment with the JAK1/2 inhibitor ruxolitinib (Fridman et al., 2010) precluded p-STAT3 and LEF1 upregulation in the articular region of P1-Pit::DTR mice (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–A').
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–A', and citation to Fridman et al., 2010.

claim: Ruxolitinib failed to rescue bone growth in P1-Pit::DTR mice.
source: However, like IGF1 injection, ruxolitinib failed to rescue bone growth (Figure 6A–B, n = 5), perhaps because mTORC1 signaling remained downregulated in the pre-HZ (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C').
evidence: The claim is supported by bone length measurement data shown in Figure 6A–B and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C'.

claim: The combined treatment of ruxolitinib and intraarticular IGF1 had a significant rescue effect on bone growth in P1-Pit::DTR mice.
source: Finally, we tested whether redundancies exist between the fat pad-HZ axis and the pAC-RZ axis by administering ruxolitinib and intraarticular IGF1 either individually or in combination in the same litters. Notably, unlike single treatments, the combined treatment had a significant rescue effect (Figure 6A–B), although only some femora (3 out of 11) and none of the tibiae showed complete rescue (see Discussion).
evidence: The claim is supported by bone length measurement data shown in Figure 6A–B.

claim: Only some femora (3 out of 11) and none of the tibiae showed complete rescue after combined treatment with ruxolitinib and IGF1.
source: Finally, we tested whether redundancies exist between the fat pad-HZ axis and the pAC-RZ axis by administering ruxolitinib and intraarticular IGF1 either individually or in combination in the same litters. Notably, unlike single treatments, the combined treatment had a significant rescue effect (Figure 6A–B), although only some femora (3 out of 11) and none of the tibiae showed complete rescue (see Discussion).
evidence: The claim is supported by bone length measurement data shown in Figure 6A–B.

claim: Analysis of cell death 3-4dpi in P14-Pit::DTR mice revealed apoptotic cells only in the surrounding soft tissues, and not the GP.
source: Similar to the P1 injections, analysis of cell death 3-4dpi in P14-Pit::DTR mice revealed apoptotic cells only in the surrounding soft tissues, and not the GP (Figure 7A, n = 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by TUNEL staining data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The height of the left HZ zone at 4dpi was reduced in P14-Pit::DTR mice compared to controls.
source: As in the P1-Pit::DTR model, the height of the left HZ zone at 4dpi was reduced in P14-Pit::DTR mice compared to controls (Figure 7B, n = 2), and the hindlimbs developed a progressive left-right asymmetry over time, although it was non-significant at P20 (~7–13% by P57, Figure 7F–G, n = 3–4 per genotype at P20, n = 7 per genotype at P57).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The hindlimbs of P14-Pit::DTR mice developed a progressive left-right asymmetry over time, although it was non-significant at P20 (~7–13% by P57).
source: As in the P1-Pit::DTR model, the height of the left HZ zone at 4dpi was reduced in P14-Pit::DTR mice compared to controls (Figure 7B, n = 2), and the hindlimbs developed a progressive left-right asymmetry over time, although it was non-significant at P20 (~7–13% by P57, Figure 7F–G, n = 3–4 per genotype at P20, n = 7 per genotype at P57).
evidence: The claim is supported by bone length measurement data shown in Figure 7F–G.

claim: Although neutrophils infiltrated the knee joint in P14-Pit::DTR mice, mTORC1 activity and Ihh signaling were not reduced at 3-4dpi in the left HZ as compared to the right.
source: Furthermore, although neutrophils infiltrated the knee joint, mTORC1 activity and Ihh signaling were not reduced at 3-4dpi in the left HZ as compared to the right in P14-Pit::DTR mice, unlike in the P1-Pit::DTR experiment (Figure 7C, n = 4 and not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Igf1 is no longer expressed in the right nor the left IPFP at P17-18.
source: Interestingly, we found that Igf1 is no longer expressed in the right nor the left IPFP at P17-18 (Figure 7D, inset, n = 3), suggesting that mTORC1 activity in the HZ eventually becomes independent of this extrinsic source of IGF1.
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Similar to P1-Pit::DTR mice, Egr1 and LEF1 were ectopically activated in the left cartilage of P14-Pit::DTR mice.
source: On the other hand, similar to P1-Pit::DTR mice, Egr1 and LEF1 were ectopically activated in the left cartilage of P14-Pit::DTR mice (Figure 7D–E, n = 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by in situ hybridization and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7D–E.

claim: The IPFP appeared as a defined region at around E17.5.
source: The IPFP appeared as a defined region at around E17.5, and this coincided with the accumulation of a high level of Igf1 expression in the area as compared to the surrounding mesenchymal tissues.
evidence: The claim is based on histological and in situ hybridization analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The appearance of the IPFP at E17.5 coincided with the accumulation of a high level of Igf1 expression in the area as compared to the surrounding mesenchymal tissues.
source: The IPFP appeared as a defined region at around E17.5, and this coincided with the accumulation of a high level of Igf1 expression in the area as compared to the surrounding mesenchymal tissues.
evidence: The claim is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Perivascular stem cells (CD44/CD90+) were detected in the interzone area even before the IPFP was formed.
source: While perivascular stem cells (CD44/CD90+) (Hindle et al., 2017) were detected in the interzone area even before the IPFP was formed, adipocytes (detected either by hematoxylin and eosin staining or expression of FABP4) were not clearly seen until P3-P4, indicating that adipocytes are not the main source of Igf1.
evidence: The claim is based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, and citation to Hindle et al., 2017.

claim: Adipocytes were not clearly seen in the IPFP until P3-P4, indicating that adipocytes are not the main source of Igf1.
source: While perivascular stem cells (CD44/CD90+) (Hindle et al., 2017) were detected in the interzone area even before the IPFP was formed, adipocytes (detected either by hematoxylin and eosin staining or expression of FABP4) were not clearly seen until P3-P4, indicating that adipocytes are not the main source of Igf1.
evidence: The claim is based on histological and immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Igf1 expression levels gradually decreased postnatally until they were barely detectable at P8 and not detected at P12.
source: As expected, Igf1 expression levels gradually decreased postnatally until they were barely detectable at P8 and not detected at P12.
evidence: The claim is based on in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The radius grows more slowly than the tibia at the stages when Igf1 levels are high in the IPFP, whereas the ratio stabilizes after P8, roughly coinciding with the cessation of Igf1 expression.
source: Intrigued by the dynamic expression of Igf1 in the IPFP, we finally explored whether the dynamics correlate with any change in the ratio of the lengths of the radius (far from any fat pad, see Figure 7—figure supplement 1A') and the tibia during development. Interestingly, we observed that the radius grows more slowly than the tibia at the stages when Igf1 levels are high in the IPFP, whereas the ratio stabilizes after P8, roughly coinciding with the cessation of Igf1 expression (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by bone length ratio measurements shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Transient cell death in the early postnatal left hindlimb mesenchyme surrounding the GPs leads to reduced long bone growth due to altered signaling from two tissues in the adjacent knee joint.
source: Our study demonstrates that transient cell death in the early postnatal left hindlimb mesenchyme surrounding the GPs leads to reduced long bone growth due to altered signaling from two tissues in the adjacent knee joint.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the entire set of experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TGFβR2 signaling from the joint interzone stimulates chondrocyte hypertrophy in the GP.
source: Only a few recent studies have addressed the regulation of longitudinal bone growth by the surrounding tissues, and showed that TGFβR2 signaling from the joint interzone stimulates chondrocyte hypertrophy in the GP (Longobardi et al., 2012), and FGFs produced by the perichondrium negatively modulate bone growth in a GP non-autonomous fashion (Liu et al., 2002; Karuppaiah et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Longobardi et al., 2012.

claim: FGFs produced by the perichondrium negatively modulate bone growth in a GP non-autonomous fashion.
source: Only a few recent studies have addressed the regulation of longitudinal bone growth by the surrounding tissues, and showed that TGFβR2 signaling from the joint interzone stimulates chondrocyte hypertrophy in the GP (Longobardi et al., 2012), and FGFs produced by the perichondrium negatively modulate bone growth in a GP non-autonomous fashion (Liu et al., 2002; Karuppaiah et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2002; Karuppaiah et al., 2016.

claim: The study identifies two neonatal joint components that can modulate bone growth, at least following injury: the IPFP and the pAC/AC.
source: Of significance, our study identifies two neonatal joint components that can modulate bone growth, at least following injury: the IPFP and the pAC/AC.
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Extrinsic signals from the IPFP and/or pAC/AC modulate distinct GP-intrinsic signaling pathways, leading to reduced bone growth, even in the absence of intrinsic damage to the GP.
source: Taken together, our data support a model whereby extrinsic signals from the IPFP and/or pAC/AC modulate distinct GP-intrinsic signaling pathways, leading to reduced bone growth, even in the absence of intrinsic damage to the GP (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: The claim is a summary statement supported by the experimental data and model shown in Figure 6C–D.

claim: The apparently milder rescue of the tibia compared to the femur could mean that each bone's response to the same growth-modulating cues varies with the developmental stage in a different manner.
source: While we think this model can be generally applied, the apparently milder rescue of the tibia compared to the femur (Figure 6B) could mean that each bone's response to the same growth-modulating cues varies with the developmental stage in a different manner.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the rescue experiment data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The specific effect of limb immobilization on the growth of different bones has recently been shown to depend on the time of treatment in chicken and crocodile embryos.
source: Indeed, the specific effect of limb immobilization on the growth of different bones has recently been shown to depend on the time of treatment in chicken and crocodile embryos (Pollard et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Pollard et al., 2017.

claim: Pro-inflammatory cytokines can exert a negative influence on bone growth that continues well beyond the cytokine exposure period.
source: This result is reminiscent of in vitro studies showing that pro-inflammatory cytokines can exert a negative influence on bone growth that continues well beyond the cytokine exposure period (MacRae et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to MacRae et al., 2006.

claim: The inflammation-dependent in vitro growth defect was only partially rescued by IGF1 treatment.
source: As in our in vivo study, the inflammation-dependent in vitro growth defect was only partially rescued by IGF1 treatment (Mårtensson et al., 2004), suggesting that inflammation impairs bone growth via both IGF-dependent and -independent pathways.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mårtensson et al., 2004.

claim: Loss of mTORC1 signaling in the pre-HZ correlates with loss of Ihh expression in P1-Pit::DTR mice.
source: Using our P1-Pit::DTR mice, we also uncovered that loss of mTORC1 signaling in the pre-HZ correlates with loss of Ihh expression, and that restoration of IGF1 levels in the joint rescues both pathways.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data showing correlation between mTORC1 and Ihh signaling.

claim: Restoration of IGF1 levels in the joint rescues both mTORC1 and Ihh signaling pathways.
source: Using our P1-Pit::DTR mice, we also uncovered that loss of mTORC1 signaling in the pre-HZ correlates with loss of Ihh expression, and that restoration of IGF1 levels in the joint rescues both pathways.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data showing IGF1 injection rescues mTORC1 and Ihh signaling.

claim: SHP2 inhibition in P1-Pit::DTR mice rescues Ihh expression but not mTORC1 activity.
source: At the same time, SHP2 inhibition in P1-Pit::DTR mice rescues Ihh expression but not mTORC1 activity, and mTORC1 inhibition does not reduce Ihh expression in WT animals (Sanchez et al., 2009), nor does it impair IGF1-mediated rescue of Ihh expression in Pit::DTR mice (Figure 4B'').
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B'' and citation to Sanchez et al., 2009.

claim: mTORC1 inhibition does not reduce Ihh expression in WT animals.
source: At the same time, SHP2 inhibition in P1-Pit::DTR mice rescues Ihh expression but not mTORC1 activity, and mTORC1 inhibition does not reduce Ihh expression in WT animals (Sanchez et al., 2009), nor does it impair IGF1-mediated rescue of Ihh expression in Pit::DTR mice (Figure 4B'').
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sanchez et al., 2009.

claim: mTORC1 inhibition does not impair IGF1-mediated rescue of Ihh expression in Pit::DTR mice.
source: At the same time, SHP2 inhibition in P1-Pit::DTR mice rescues Ihh expression but not mTORC1 activity, and mTORC1 inhibition does not reduce Ihh expression in WT animals (Sanchez et al., 2009), nor does it impair IGF1-mediated rescue of Ihh expression in Pit::DTR mice (Figure 4B'').
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B''.

claim: IGF1 activates Ihh expression via an mTORC1-independent pathway, possibly by inhibition of SHP2.
source: Therefore, we speculate that IGF1 activates Ihh expression via an mTORC1-independent pathway, possibly by inhibition of SHP2 (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference based on the experimental data, as indicated by the word 'speculate'.

claim: The requirement of IGF signaling for Ihh expression seems to be restricted to a narrow perinatal window.
source: Notably, the requirement of IGF signaling for Ihh expression seems to be restricted to a narrow perinatal window, as Igf1r deletion in the cartilage only reduces Ihh expression when triggered at P5 but not prenatally (Wang et al., 2011), and we show that Igf1 is no longer expressed in the IPFP by P12.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2011 and the experimental data showing Igf1 expression dynamics.

claim: Igf1r deletion in the cartilage only reduces Ihh expression when triggered at P5 but not prenatally.
source: Notably, the requirement of IGF signaling for Ihh expression seems to be restricted to a narrow perinatal window, as Igf1r deletion in the cartilage only reduces Ihh expression when triggered at P5 but not prenatally (Wang et al., 2011), and we show that Igf1 is no longer expressed in the IPFP by P12.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2011.

claim: mTORC1 was induced in the left pAC and RZ of P1-Pit::DTR mice despite reduction of local IGF1 levels.
source: Unlike in the pre-HZ, we found mTORC1 activity was increased in the left pAC and RZ of P1-Pit::DTR mice. Since mTORC1 was induced despite reduction of local IGF1 levels, it follows that another signal must be responsible for mTORC1 activation in the AC/RZ.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data showing increased p-S6 in the pAC and RZ despite reduced Igf1.

claim: IL6 expressed ectopically in the AC is a candidate signal responsible for mTORC1 activation in the AC/RZ, as this cytokine can activate mTORC1 in some cell types.
source: One candidate is IL6 expressed ectopically in the AC, as this cytokine can activate mTORC1 in some cell types (Kim et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference based on the experimental data and citation to Kim et al., 2008.

claim: Inhibition of mTORC1 activity dampened LEF1 levels in the RZ without impairing STAT3 phosphorylation.
source: Interestingly, inhibition of mTORC1 activity dampened LEF1 levels in the RZ without impairing STAT3 phosphorylation, (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A'', C''), while JAK1/2 inhibition also precluded LEF1 upregulation, without impeding p-S6 activation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A',C').
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A'', C''.

claim: JAK1/2 inhibition precluded LEF1 upregulation, without impeding p-S6 activation.
source: Interestingly, inhibition of mTORC1 activity dampened LEF1 levels in the RZ without impairing STAT3 phosphorylation, (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A'', C''), while JAK1/2 inhibition also precluded LEF1 upregulation, without impeding p-S6 activation (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A',C').
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A', C'.

claim: Both mTORC1 and JAK/STAT signaling pathways are independently required to activate Lef1 expression.
source: These results suggest that both mTORC1 and JAK/STAT signaling pathways are independently required to activate Lef1 expression (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and summarized in Figure 6E.

claim: The local influence exerted by the joint region could at least in part explain the fact that the proximal tibia and distal femur GPs grow faster than the distal tibia or proximal femur.
source: We speculate that the local influence exerted by the joint region could at least in part explain poorly understood phenomena observed in the field of bone growth, such as the fact that the proximal tibia and distal femur GPs (i.e. closest to the fat pad) grow faster than the distal tibia or proximal femur (Digby, 1916; Payton, 1932; Moss-Salentijn, 1974).
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference based on the experimental findings and citations to Digby, 1916; Payton, 1932; Moss-Salentijn, 1974.

claim: Differential GP growth has been recently suggested to be evolutionary optimized to achieve energy-efficient scaling of the growing bones by minimizing the remodeling of ossified cortical structures.
source: Our proposal is biologically relevant because differential GP growth has been recently suggested to be evolutionary optimized to achieve energy-efficient scaling of the growing bones by minimizing the remodeling of ossified cortical structures (Stern et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Stern et al., 2015.

claim: Classic experiments showed a change in growth rate upon proximo-distal transposition of the GPs within a bone, strongly suggesting the involvement of local extrinsic factors.
source: While intrinsic differences in the GP likely exist and account in part for differential growth of proximal and distal GPs, classic experiments showed a change in growth rate upon proximo-distal transposition of the GPs within a bone (Moss-Salentijn, 1974; Hert, 1964), strongly suggesting the involvement of local extrinsic factors.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Moss-Salentijn, 1974; Hert, 1964.

claim: Adipocyte-secreted signals can stimulate long bone growth in the absence of growth hormone.
source: Fat pads are probably one of the main participants in this process, as suggested by our study and those of others showing that adipocyte-secreted signals can stimulate long bone growth in the absence of growth hormone (Shtaif et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Shtaif et al., 2015.

claim: The finding that Igf1 is almost absent from the IPFP by P8 correlates with the fact that the femur and tibia grow faster than the rest of the body (including forelimb bones) until roughly the same stage.
source: In this regard, our finding that Igf1 is almost absent from the IPFP by P8 correlates with the fact that the femur and tibia grow faster than the rest of the body (including forelimb bones) until roughly the same stage (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and [Roselló-Díez and Joyner, 2015]).
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and citation to Roselló-Díez and Joyner, 2015.

claim: The GP likely becomes independent from the IPFP after ~P8 due both to the intervening presence of the secondary ossification center as well as to cessation of Igf1 expression in the fat pad.
source: The GP likely becomes independent from the IPFP after ~P8 (due both to the intervening presence of the secondary ossification center as well as to cessation of Igf1 expression in the fat pad), which could also explain why it takes longer for bone growth to be significantly impaired when the injury is induced at P14 vs. P1.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data comparing P1 and P14 injury models.

claim: Local tissues hosting cells with osteochondrogenic potential, such as the synovium, bone marrow or the perichondrial groove of Ranvier, can contribute to bone growth not only with paracrine signals, but also with progenitor cells.
source: Finally, we cannot exclude the possibility that the IPFP and/or other local tissues hosting cells with osteochondrogenic potential, such as the synovium, bone marrow or the perichondrial groove of Ranvier (Hindle et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2013; Karlsson et al., 2009; Chung and Xian, 2014), can contribute to bone growth not only with paracrine signals, but also with progenitor cells (see for example Fig. S9 in [Yang et al., 2013]), such that cell death within these tissues in Pit::DTR mice depletes a pool of cells that participates in recovery of the injured bones.
evidence: The claim is a speculative inference based on citations to Hindle et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2013; Karlsson et al., 2009; Chung and Xian, 2014.
